title: Cherry Hills Village well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Cherry Hills Village, median well depth is 33 ft with a 16 ft median water level. Learn about local well yields, costs, and drilling risks.
h1: Wells and drilling in Cherry Hills Village, Colorado
intro_html: Cherry Hills Village sits over the Denver Basin system, but most nearby wells are surprisingly shallow. Within about 5 miles, records show thousands of mostly monitoring and domestic wells in Denver County and nearby Greenwood Village and Englewood. If you are buying a home on a well or thinking about new construction, the state data give a pretty clear picture of how deep you are likely to go and how much water you can expect.

sections.heading: How deep wells go around Cherry Hills Village
sections.html:
State records near Cherry Hills Village show a median total depth of 33 feet, with the middle half of wells between 22 and 59 feet. That means a lot of holes in this area are essentially shallow Denver Basin alluvial or weathered bedrock completions, not the deep municipal-style wells you see farther out on the plains.

It is not all shallow, though. About 10% of wells go deeper than 600 feet, the 90th percentile depth stretches to 723 feet, and the deepest well on record hits 2,200 feet. So while most domestic or small irrigation wells stay under 100 feet (82% of wells), there is a real tail of very deep Denver aquifer completions that carry very different costs.

sections.heading: Well yields and how much water you can expect
sections.html:
For yield, the numbers near Cherry Hills Village are generally favorable. The median reported pump rate is 15 gallons per minute, and the middle half runs from 8.8 to 52.5 gpm. Over half of the measured wells (52%) produce more than 15 gpm, and another 34% fall between 5 and 15 gpm, which is plenty for a standard exempt household well and then some.

The problem cases are there but not common: about 3% of wells report under 1 gpm and 11% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. Those low producers can still work for indoor household use with storage, but they are a red flag if you are planning heavy irrigation or multiple dwellings on one well.

sections.heading: Water levels and what they say about the local aquifer
sections.html:
Depth to water in this area is typically shallow. The median static water level is 16 feet below ground surface, and the middle half of readings sit between 12 and 27 feet. That is consistent with the high share of relatively shallow completions and the influence of alluvial material over Denver Basin bedrock.

Looking at trend, the median measured water level was about 17 feet in the 2010s and 13 feet in the 2020s. That is a small shift toward shallower water in the recent data, not a drop. With 100% of wells in the records tied to the Denver Basin aquifer system (including fractured-bedrock and alluvial settings), this suggests the local water table has been relatively stable in the short term, at least where it is being measured.

sections.heading: Who is drilling here and when wells went in
sections.html:
Within about 5 miles of Cherry Hills Village there are 7,312 well permits on record, with 3,392 shown as constructed and 4,094 reporting a total depth. Most are not houses on small acreage; roughly 58% are monitoring wells, with domestic or household wells at about 16%, irrigation at 6%, and a small amount of stock use.

Drilling activity picked up sharply in the 1990s and 2000s. The state shows 1,814 permits issued in the 1990s and 1,975 in the 2000s, compared to under 300 per decade before 1980. Activity has tapered some since, with 724 permits in the 2010s and 390 so far in the 2020s, including a newest permit year of 2025. The busiest outfits in the records are Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 2,860 wells, Hier Drilling Co Inc with 194, and Ground Exploration LLC with 135.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Cherry Hills Village
sections.html:
Here the ground is mainly Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, and local drillers typically bid in the $50–$70 per foot range. At the median depth of 33 feet, the drilled hole alone comes out around $1,600–$2,300. By the time you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical, a finished shallow well is often in the $7,600–$14,300 range.

The catch is that you cannot assume you will land at 33 feet. The 10% of wells going past 600 feet and individual holes down to 2,200 feet show what happens when a site needs a true Denver aquifer completion. On those deeper jobs, both drilling and pump costs rise fast, so any bid should spell out per‑foot pricing and what happens if they have to keep going.

sections.heading: Risks to look at: contamination, low yield, and construction issues
sections.html:
Being close to Denver, the big concern here is not just low yield. Within about 10 miles of Cherry Hills Village there are 455 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 144 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, plus 7 mapped historic mine features. That level of industrial and urban history means water testing for PFAS and other contaminants is not optional; it is part of due diligence.

On the water supply side, only a small slice of wells come in under 1 gpm or in the 1–5 gpm band, but they exist. Before you buy, look up neighboring well permits and yields and confirm you have room for proper well and septic setbacks on the lot. Shallow water also makes sanitary sealing and grout work important so surface impacts from nearby development do not end up in your well.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Cherry Hills Village
sections.html:
If you are buying an existing home on a private well near Cherry Hills Village, start with the permit record: depth, yield, static level, and which aquifer is listed (fractured bedrock, alluvial, or Denver). With a median depth of 33 feet and a median yield of 15 gpm in the area, most systems have good potential, but lab testing for PFAS and other urban contaminants should be part of any inspection.

For a vacant parcel around Greenwood Village, Holly Hills, Englewood, or Sheridan, budget both for the shallow case and the possibility of a deeper Denver Basin well. Talk to a local driller about nearby completions, not just the averages, and sort out your well location, septic layout, and access early in the design so everything meets state and county spacing rules.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Cherry Hills Village, Colorado?
faq.a: Near Cherry Hills Village the median well depth is about 33 feet, and the middle half of wells fall between 22 and 59 feet. Most holes are quite shallow, with 82% of wells under 100 feet. However, around 10% of wells go deeper than 600 feet, the 90th percentile is 723 feet, and one recorded well reaches 2,200 feet, so deeper Denver aquifer completions do exist.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce around Cherry Hills Village?
faq.a: Reported yields near Cherry Hills Village are generally strong. The median pump rate is 15 gpm, with the middle half from 8.8 to 52.5 gpm. Over half of measured wells produce more than 15 gpm, and about a third fall between 5 and 15 gpm. Roughly 14% are below 5 gpm, including about 3% under 1 gpm, which may require storage and conservation planning.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Cherry Hills Village?
faq.a: In the Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock around Cherry Hills Village, drilling typically runs $50–$70 per foot. At the local median depth of about 33 feet, the drilled hole might cost roughly $1,600–$2,300, and a complete system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical often totals around $7,600–$14,300. Deeper Denver aquifer wells, which can exceed 600 feet, will increase that cost significantly.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Cherry Hills Village?
faq.a: Safety depends on testing, not just depth. Within about 10 miles of Cherry Hills Village there are 455 PFAS sampling or contamination sites and 144 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites, plus 7 historic mine features. Those numbers reflect a complex urban and industrial history. Any private well here should be tested for PFAS, basic potability, and common urban contaminants before you rely on it for drinking water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Cherry Hills Village, Colorado?
faq.a: Available records do not show a recent drop in measured water levels. The median static water level is about 16 feet below ground, with most readings between 12 and 27 feet. By decade, median depth to water was roughly 17 feet in the 2010s and 13 feet in the 2020s, which is actually a shift toward shallower water in the recent data, suggesting a relatively stable local table where it is monitored.
